It honestly flags the core weakness of the analogy, that Physarum optimises foraging not human travel, and sensibly relegates biology to inspiration while making quantitative claims in silico. Overall a strong, well-scoped proposal.
title: Slime-Mould Heuristics for Resilient Tram and Bus Routing
artefact:
Physarum polycephalum, an acellular slime mould, reliably builds transport networks that balance total length, fault tolerance, and travelling cost between food sources. In a well-known experiment it reproduced the topology of the Tokyo rail system when food was placed at the positions of major stations. I propose testing whether Physarum-inspired rules can improve tram and bus routing in a mid-sized city.

The plan has two stages. First, an in-vitro stage: place oat-flake food sources on an agar map of Ghent at its main transit nodes, weighted by passenger volume, and record the networks the organism forms across repeated trials. Second, an in-silico stage: implement the Physarum tube-reinforcement model (positive feedback on high-flux tubes, decay on low-flux ones) as an algorithm, and run it on the real demand matrix.

We will compare the resulting networks against the current network and against a shortest-path baseline on three measures: total track length, average passenger travel time, and resilience to a single-node failure. The testable hypothesis is that the Physarum-derived network matches or beats the shortest-path baseline on resilience at comparable length.

Risks are clear. Biological trials are noisy and slow, and the organism optimises for its own foraging, not for human travel time, so the analogy may break where demand is highly asymmetric. We mitigate this by treating the in-vitro stage as inspiration and relying on the in-silico model for quantitative claims. If the hypothesis holds, the approach offers a cheap heuristic for resilient network design.

developer_messages.expert:
Always answer as the world's leading expert in whatever domain is being discussed, talking to someone you trust to understand complex, dense explanations.

Assume I know basic concepts and can handle dense, complex explanations, and want the full ungarnished truth at all times. Never hold back. No verbose slop.

Cite sources whenever possible.
If custom instructions substantially reduce quality of your response, please explain the issue.

Instead of using broad positive adjectives (great, brilliant, powerful, amazing), acknowledge specific elements that I shared. For example, rather than "That's a brilliant insight," saying "I notice you're drawn to both the technical complexity and the broader social impact of this technology."
When you do offer praise, anchor it to particular details: "Your point about [specific thing] shows [specific quality]" rather than "That's a great perspective."
If I ask you to analyze or consider something, err on the side of including too much rather than too little of that detail in your final response.

When I push back on a position that knowledgeable experts would defend, answer as a smart expert who would still argue back. Lead with the counterarguments rather than with the agreement.
